name: Brow tweezers + scissors
lead: Brow tweezers and small grooming scissors are hand tools used to shape the eyebrows. Tweezers grip individual hairs and pull them out, typically to remove strays below, between or above the brow line, while small scissors trim hairs that grow longer than the rest. Tweezers are among the oldest grooming implements, with archaeological finds from ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia and Rome. [1][6]

People use the tools to give the brows a defined, tidy edge. Practitioners and grooming guides describe clean brows as framing the eyes and changing how the upper face reads, and brow cleanup is often cited in looksmaxxing communities as one of the cheapest changes available for the eye area. The effect appears immediately and lasts until the hairs regrow, a matter of weeks. [2][8]

Brow grooming sits in a wider family of methods that includes waxing, threading, tinting, brow pencils, microblading and brow transplants, and tweezers and scissors are the lowest-cost and most easily reversed of these. [7][10][12][13] Eyebrow fashion has swung between thin and full several times over the centuries, from Heian-era Japanese hikimayu to the pencil-thin brows of the 1920s and 1930s. [7][11]

The tools are inexpensive, non-prescription consumer goods. No published study has tested brow tweezers or scissors as an appearance intervention, so the research base consists of general hair-removal literature, a small study on eyebrow regrowth, and dermatologist commentary on over-plucking. [2][3][14]

angle.text: Tweezers remove stray hairs below, between and above the brows, and scissors shorten hairs that extend past the brow line. The change is visible straight away and is used to sharpen the frame around the eyes. Results last until the hair regrows.

infobox: Cleaning of tool tips; periodic repeat grooming

paras: Tweezers are two-armed pincers joined at one end, usually of stainless steel, with slanted, pointed or flat tips depending on the intended use. They are essentially thumb-driven forceps: two levers meet at a fixed end and spring tension holds the tips apart until finger pressure closes them. They can be made from two fused pieces, which is described as giving a stronger grip at higher cost, or from one bent piece of metal, which is cheaper. [6] Brow scissors are small, often curved or angled blades used with a spoolie or comb to trim hair that extends beyond the brow line. [1]

Tweezing is a form of epilation, meaning the hair is removed along with its bulb, whereas trimming or shaving only removes the shaft. A 2021 literature review on hair-removal practices classes plucking among epilatory methods and notes that all common methods except electrolysis are temporary. [2]

Tweezing is the most common method for thinning and shaping the brows, alongside waxing, threading (a twisted cotton thread that pulls hairs out) and trimming with scissors, which is used on its own or together with other methods. Makeup, brow transplants, microblading and, since the 1970s, botulinum toxin injections to lift the brow are other approaches to the area. [7]

Archaeological evidence cited in reference works places tweezers in Egypt by the early dynastic period, in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley by roughly 3000 to 2000 BCE, and in Roman toilet kits, where more than fifty examples were reportedly found near baths at Wroxeter in Britain. [1] Gold tweezers were found in the Royal Cemetery of Ur, dated to about 2550 to 2450 BCE. [6] The English word is traced to a small carrying case, the 'etwee', in which such implements were kept. [6]

Fashions in brow shape have shifted repeatedly and have often been tied to cultural expectations about body hair. Wikipedia's eyebrow article records that Japanese women and men from the 8th century practised hikimayu, shaving or plucking the brows and painting them higher on the forehead; that some high-status women in Elizabethan England removed their brows entirely; and that thin pencil-line brows were fashionable in the 1920s and 1930s. Thick brows later became associated with figures such as Audrey Hepburn. [7]

Hikimayu, the Japanese practice of removing the natural brows and painting them higher on the forehead, appeared in the 8th century as the court adopted Chinese styles, and reportedly made it easier to apply white face powder. Over the Heian period it shifted to ovals or smudges drawn above the natural line, men at court later adopted it, and by the Edo period (1603 to 1867) it was limited to married women. It was banned in 1870 as Japan adopted Western customs. [11]

Threading, in which a doubled twisted cotton thread is rolled over unwanted hairs, has been practised for centuries in the Middle East and South Asia, in some places as preparation for marriage. Wikipedia credits an Iranian beautician, Parastu Amiri, with introducing it in Germany in the 1980s, and reports that immigrant-run studios brought it to US cities in the late 1980s. The Guardian reported that UK online searches for threading rose 50 percent in 2015 and described brows as the beauty obsession of the decade. [10]

Plucking removes the hair from the follicle, so the hair must regrow from the base; visible regrowth is commonly described as taking several weeks. Scissors leave the root untouched, so the hair continues to grow and requires repeat trimming. [2]

Eyebrows serve to keep sweat and debris out of the eyes and, according to reference summaries of recent research, to communicate expression, since mobile, visible brows convey subtle emotion. [7] Grooming changes the outline of this structure without altering the underlying hair pattern.

Waxing uses sticky wax that grips hairs and removes them from the root. Wikipedia reports regrowth typically takes several weeks and that some people notice softer regrowth after long periods of waxing. Listed drawbacks include pain, redness, ingrown hairs and, in people using blood thinners, immunosuppressants or retinoids or with certain skin conditions, an increased chance of skin lifting. [13]

Threading removes short rows of hairs at once rather than single hairs. Proponents cite precise shaping and gentler treatment of the skin than waxing; sources describe it as painful because several hairs go at a time. [10]

Microblading is a semi-permanent tattoo technique that draws hair-like strokes into the upper dermis and may last up to about two years. Wikipedia describes cosmetic eyebrow tattooing growing in the US and Asia in the 1980s and 1990s and microblading becoming popular in the US and Canada by the mid-2010s, with complications such as pigment migration, colour change and, rarely, granulomatous reactions. [12] Tinting and brow pencils are temporary ways to change colour or fill sparse areas. [8][9]

Because the result is simply the removal or shortening of hairs, it is immediate and temporary. No trials have measured perceived attractiveness or eye-area appearance before and after brow tweezing or trimming.

A small randomized study of five patients, in which one eyebrow was completely shaved and the other left as a control, found full regrowth within six months in all participants and observers could not reliably identify the shaved side. The authors noted slower regrowth in one woman with sparser, lighter brow hair. The study concerned shaving, not plucking, and was very small. [3]

Reported effects of plucking in the hair-removal literature include redness, irritation, ingrown hairs and folliculitis, and unclean tools can contribute to infection. [2] Proponents of conservative plucking commonly say that over-plucking can leave brows thin for a long period; the controlled data on permanent loss from plucking are limited, and the shaving study above observed regrowth. [3] Hair removal methods are also described as causing brief pain, which many people report lessening with habit. [7]

Brow thinning can also have medical causes unrelated to grooming. Frontal fibrosing alopecia and alopecia areata can affect the eyebrows, and clinicians distinguish these from cosmetic over-plucking. A 2022 pair of phase 3 trials of baricitinib studied alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that can involve the scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes. [4][5]

Dermatologists quoted by NBC News in 2011 described the risk of long-term thinning. Carolyn Jacob of Chicago said over-plucking can shrink the follicle so regrowing hairs come in finer, and Paradi Mirmirani of California said forceful plucking or chronic irritation can scar a follicle, calling that outcome rare and permanent once it occurs. [14] General hair-removal references list inflammation, ingrown hairs, bumps and folliculitis among the risks of epilation. [15]

In grooming guides, the standard approach is to remove only obvious strays beneath and between the brows and to trim long hairs while leaving the natural shape. Forum participants often describe brow cleanup as one of the cheapest changes available for the eye area, and looksmax.org has long-running threads on eyebrow shape, grooming and thickness, including one titled for the view that brows matter more than is usually thought, for both facial attractiveness and nonverbal communication. [8][9][17]

Threads on sparse brows discuss pencil and dye use, derma rolling, and growth approaches such as castor oil, peptide serums and minoxidil; participants disagree about which they find effective. [9][16] Members also post cautionary accounts: one user wrote that using his mother's brow pencil left the brows looking heavily made up and hard to remove, an example of why many discussions favour subtle changes. [8]

Common product variations are slant-tip, point-tip and flat-tip tweezers and straight or curved scissors. Features commonly mentioned include tips that meet evenly and materials that can be cleaned or disinfected. Tweezers of one-piece construction are described as lower in cost and with a weaker grip than fused two-piece designs. [6]

No studies found that evaluate brow tweezers or scissors specifically. Related research includes a small randomized trial of eyebrow shaving and regrowth, and broader reviews of hair-removal methods. [2][3] In that trial, five patients had one brow shaved at random and the other kept as a control; all showed regrowth within six months. [3] Trials of baricitinib in alopecia areata, which can involve the brows, concern a medical condition rather than grooming. [5]

timeline.event: Copper tweezers appear in Egyptian burials of the early dynastic period. [1]
Gold tweezers are deposited in the Royal Cemetery of Ur. [6]
Hikimayu brow shaving and repainting is adopted at the Japanese court. [11]
Hikimayu is banned in Japan as Western customs are adopted. [11]
Thin pencil-line brows are in fashion. [7]
Threading is introduced to Germany and spreads across Europe; cosmetic eyebrow tattooing grows in the US and Asia. [10][12]
Immigrant-run studios bring threading to US cities. [10]
A small randomized study reports full eyebrow regrowth after complete shaving. [3]
NBC News quotes dermatologists on follicle damage from over-plucking. [14]
Microblading becomes popular in the US and Canada. [12]
UK online searches for threading services reportedly rise 50 percent. [10]
A review of hair-removal practices summarizes epilatory and depilatory methods. [2]

lore.intro: Brow grooming comes up on looksmax.org in threads about eye-area framing, brow shape and ways to thicken sparse brows. [8][9][17]

claims.claim: Cleaning up stray brow hairs makes the eye area look better
claims.believers: Forum users describe brows as an inexpensive, quick change that frames the eyes, and recommend removing only obvious strays. [8]
claims.experts: No published study has measured attractiveness before and after tweezing or trimming; hair-removal reviews describe the technique and its effects as temporary. [2]

claims.claim: Brows matter more for facial attractiveness and communication than people think
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues brows are underrated for both attractiveness and nonverbal communication. [17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's eyebrow article says brows keep sweat and debris from the eyes and convey expression; it does not report trials of brow grooming and attractiveness. [7]

claims.claim: Castor oil, peptides or minoxidil can thicken thin brows
claims.believers: Users in eyebrow threads report using castor oil, brow growth peptides or minoxidil, with some saying peptides or minoxidil gave better results than castor oil. [9][16]
claims.experts: The brow-specific literature located covers shaving and regrowth and alopecia treatments, not these cosmetic regimens; no trial of them for brow thickness is cited. [3][5]

claims.claim: Over-plucking can leave brows thin permanently
claims.believers: Proponents of conservative grooming say heavy plucking can leave sparse brows for a long time.
claims.experts: Dermatologists quoted in 2011 said over-plucking can shrink follicles and that scarring is rare but permanent; a small shaving study observed full regrowth within six months. [14][3]

claims.claim: Threading gives a more precise shape than tweezing
claims.believers: Proponents cited by Wikipedia say threading is more precise and gentler on the skin than waxing, and removes short rows of hairs at once. [10]
claims.experts: The sources located are descriptive and journalistic; no comparative trial of threading and tweezing for brow shaping is cited. [10]

claims.claim: Microblading or tinting is a longer-lasting alternative for sparse brows
claims.believers: Practitioners present semi-permanent pigment as filling sparse areas for up to about two years. [12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports complications including pigment migration, colour change and granulomas, notes that US microblading is not federally regulated, and says training reduces the risk of poor outcomes. [12]
